title: Simple letters specialize from a reductive Bruhat double coset
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $G$ be a reductive affine $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme, lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]: smooth, connected and of finite type with no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup; unipotent means that geometric points are unipotent matrices in a faithful finite-dimensional representation. Fix a split maximal torus $T\subseteq B\subseteq G$, where a split torus is isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$, $r\geq0$, maximal means maximal among torus subgroups, and a Borel is a maximal smooth connected solvable closed subgroup. Solvable means that successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups become trivial. Subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], and smoothness, connectedness and finite type are as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Use the character lattice $X=X^*(T)$, roots $\Phi$, positive roots $\Phi^+$ and simple-root base $\Delta$ of [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Let $W=N_G(T)(F)/T(F)$, with its action on $X$ and reflections $s_\alpha$ as in [lem-sfb-weyl-reflection-realization]. The normalizer consists of elements conjugating $T$ to itself after every commutative algebra extension. For $w\in W$ choose a representative $n_w\in N_G(T)(F)$, and set $D_w=B(F)n_wB(F)\subseteq G(F)$. Then $W$ is generated by the $s_\alpha$ for $\alpha\in\Delta$. Call an expression $w=s_{\alpha_1}\cdots s_{\alpha_m}$ reduced if $m$ is minimal among such expressions. For every reduced expression, every $1\leq j\leq m$, and every representative $n_{s_{\alpha_j}}$, its image in the underlying topological space of $G$ belongs to the Zariski closure of the set of rational points $D_w$. Equivalently, every Zariski closed subset $Z\subseteq |G|$ containing $D_w$ contains each of these simple-reflection points. There is no semisimplicity, simply connectedness or characteristic hypothesis. Empty words and $G=T$ are allowed.

source.place: Section 21h, Theorem 21.73 and Remark 21.74 (printed p.447), Proposition 21.75 (p.448), and Appendix C.11 (p.610): Bruhat/Tits-system inputs. The simple-letter Zariski specialization is an auxiliary formulation via reduced galleries, not a verbatim assertion of 21.91; its proposed argument is recorded in report.md.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-weyl-reflection-realization], $W$ is finite and acts faithfully on $E=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf Q}\Phi$ as the group generated by root reflections. Extend to $E_{\mathbf R}$ and choose any positive definite form $q_0$; the finite sum $q(x,y)=\sum_{w\in W}q_0(wx,wy)$ is positive definite and $W$-invariant. For $s_\alpha$, its fixed hyperplane $\ker\langle-,\alpha^\vee\rangle$ is perpendicular to its minus-one line $\mathbf R\alpha$, so its coroot formula is the orthogonal reflection formula. The root datum and the base in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure] therefore satisfy all the hypotheses of [lem-sfb-simple-root-reflection-generation] on $E_{\mathbf R}$: reducedness, integrality, spanning and the simple-root sign expansions. That node identifies the root-reflection group with the simple-reflection group. Faithfulness gives $W=W_\Delta$. Hence each $w$ has a word and a least word length. If $\Phi=\varnothing$, the same faithful action gives $W=1$.

source.place: Appendix C.11, C.19--C.22, printed pp.610--612; the finite averaging formula is C.19.

proof.text: Fix $\alpha\in\Delta$. Choose $v:\operatorname{SL}_2\to G$ from [lem-sfb-opposite-root-sl2-parametrizations], and write $u_\pm(a)=v(x_\pm(a))$, $h(c)=v(\operatorname{diag}(c,c^{-1}))$. Put $J=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)=x_+(-1)x_-(1)x_+(-1)$ and $n=v(J)$. For any test algebra and $t\in T$, put $q=\alpha(t)$. The root conjugation formulas of [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations] and direct matrix multiplication give $tnt^{-1}=v(x_+(-q)x_-(q^{-1})x_+(-q))=h(q)n$. Thus $ntn^{-1}=t\alpha^\vee(\alpha(t))^{-1}$. This is an involutive automorphism of $T$, using $\alpha\circ\alpha^\vee(c)=c^2$, and on characters it is the root reflection. Hence $n\in N_G(T)(F)$ represents $s_\alpha$, by faithfulness in [lem-sfb-weyl-reflection-realization].

source.place: Theorem 21.11(d)--(e), printed pp.429--430; equation (135), p.431; paragraph 21.24, p.432. Explicit matrix calculation.

proof.text: For $a\in F^\times$, multiplication of $2\times2$ matrices gives $x_-(a)=x_+(a^{-1})J\operatorname{diag}(a,a^{-1})x_+(a^{-1})$. Apply [lem-sfb-opposite-root-sl2-parametrizations]. The positive-root inclusion of [lem-sfb-borel-root-product-coordinates] gives $u_+(a^{-1})\in B(F)$, and $h(a)\in T(F)\subseteq B(F)$. Hence $u_-(a)\in D_{s_\alpha}$. At $a=0$ the morphism $u_-:\mathbf A^1_F\to G$ takes the value $1$. Every closed $Z\subseteq|G|$ containing $D_{s_\alpha}$ therefore has inverse image containing all nonzero $F$-points of $\mathbf A^1$. This inverse image is all of $\mathbf A^1$: $F$ is infinite (a finite algebraically closed field would make $\prod_{c\in F}(X-c)-1$ a polynomial without a root), and a nonzero polynomial has only finitely many roots. Consequently $1\in\overline{D_{s_\alpha}}$.

source.place: Rank-one calculation used in Proposition 21.75, printed p.448, with paragraph 21.24, p.432. Agent specialization argument using the negative-root affine line.

proof.text: Let $w=s_{\alpha_1}\cdots s_{\alpha_m}$ be reduced, with $m\geq1$, and put $A_i=D_{s_{\alpha_i}}$. Every suffix is reduced, since a shorter expression for a suffix would shorten the whole word. Induction on $m$ gives $A_1\cdots A_m=D_w$: the case $m=1$ is the definition; for $m>1$ the suffix $v=s_{\alpha_2}\cdots s_{\alpha_m}$ has length $m-1$, its double-coset product is $D_v$ by induction, and [lem-sfb-reductive-length-increasing-bruhat-product] applies because $\ell(s_{\alpha_1}v)=\ell(v)+1$. All double cosets are independent of representatives: two representatives differ by $T(F)\subseteq B(F)$.

source.place: Proposition 21.75, printed p.448; induction along a reduced word, using only the length-increasing product.

proof.text: Here is the closure calculation on rational points, without asserting that the Zariski topology on a scheme product is the product topology. For arbitrary $A,C\subseteq G(F)$ and a closed $Z\subseteq|G|$ containing $AC$, fix $c\in C$. The inverse image of $Z$ by right translation by $c$ is closed and contains $A$, hence contains $\overline A$. Thus $ac\in Z$ for every rational $a\in\overline A$. Now fix such an $a$; the inverse image by left translation by $a$ is closed and contains $C$, hence contains $\overline C$. Therefore $ac\in Z$ for rational $a\in\overline A,c\in\overline C$. Translations are scheme morphisms by [def-sc-group-scheme], so these inverse images are closed. Intersecting over $Z$ proves $(\overline A\cap G(F))(\overline C\cap G(F))\subseteq\overline{AC}$. Inductively, the product of rational closure points of $A_1,\ldots,A_m$ lies in $\overline{A_1\cdots A_m}$.

source.place: Agent closed-inverse-image argument for translations of an algebraic group; definition of group scheme, Chapter 3, and Zariski closure.

proof.text: Fix $1\leq j\leq m$ and any representative $n_{s_{\alpha_j}}$. In the product of rational closure points from step 5, take this representative in the $j$th factor (it belongs to $A_j$), and take $1$ in every other factor, as permitted by step 3. The product is $n_{s_{\alpha_j}}$, and steps 4--5 put it in $\overline{D_w}$. This holds for every reduced word, position and representative. Membership in the closure is equivalent by definition to belonging to every closed subset containing $D_w$. If $m=0$ there is no index $j$; in particular the torus case has only this vacuous clause. None of the matrix identities divided by $2$, so the argument includes characteristic $2$.

source.place: Agent assembly of the rank-one specialization and reduced-product calculation from Proposition 21.75, printed p.448.
